articles.title_orig: Trump rejects Iran’s proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz, restart peace talks
articles.title_zh: Trump rejects Iran’s proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz, restart peace talks
articles.content_orig:
US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms
US president Donald Trump has said he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week and resume nuclear talks in return for the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
“They made a proposal but I reject it,” he told reporters at the White House.
The US president was earlier said to be privately sceptical Iran would meet his demands to dismantle its nuclear programme, according to unnamed US officials cited by the Wall Street Journal.
Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms in the US, the newspaper reported.
Meanwhile, on Friday evening, he published a post on his Truth Social platform with a graphic showing a map with the strait of Hormuz renamed as the “Trump Strait”.
During a three-hour meeting at the UN general assembly in New York earlier this week, Iran had proposed reopening the strait, which would have relieved pressure on global energy markets, and restarting talks on its nuclear programme within seven days.
In return, as well as lifting its naval blockade, Iran wants the US to permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports and observe a “ceasefire on all fronts”.
That would involve the US president convincing Israel to end its attacks on Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, a tall order, and allowing the strait to reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters.
Saudi Arabia is also said to be concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.
Reports of the rejection came as Iranian state media reported on Saturday morning that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, was on his way back to Tehran from New York.
After a meeting with UN secretary general, António Guterres, Pezeshkian said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.”
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said ⁠late on Saturday that ​Tehran had seen ⁠an initial reaction from ​Trump ‌to ‌its proposal ‌but had yet to receive a response through mediators.
Iran ‌was waiting for the mediators ​to convey the definitive US position ⁠and would ​make a ​decision ​based on ​it, he added.
Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive” and, on Friday, Araghchi, had detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council.
He said the seven-day timeline to open the strait and resume talks could start as soon as the US accepts Iran’s proposal. The initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, the strait would be opened on the sixth day and talks on the nuclear programme would start on the seventh day, he said.
This would include a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
The US naval blockade is putting intense pressure on the Iranian economy, while the seven-month-old conflict in the region has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and is increasing the cost of living around the globe.
Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks.
Since then the conflict has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy.
Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market.
The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the UN children’s agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children.
Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.
Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict.
Marina Dunbar contributed. With Reuters and AP

articles.title_zh: Indonesia eyes China for massive 2,772km railway project – with caution
articles.content_orig:
As Jakarta explores foreign backing for the Trans-Kalimantan railway, analysts say costly past ventures could shape any coming negotiations
Indonesia is considering Chinese investment to help build a massive 2,772km (1,722 mile) railway network through the vast, resource-rich region of Kalimantan, following the completion of Southeast Asia’s first high-speed line between Jakarta and Bandung, state media and analysts said.
However, analysts noted that any future commercial agreements were likely to be negotiated cautiously, given the financial strains that dogged the high-speed line and the challenges that stalled a proposed underground metro project in the congested tourist province of Bali.
The Indonesian government was “exploring” potential foreign investment to build the Trans-Kalimantan railway network, according to statements from Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi quoted by Indonesia’s official Antara news agency. The minister said China and Russia had expressed interest in the project.

President Donald Trump announced Friday that he is seeking to cancel almost $1 billion in federal funding, sidestepping congressional approval and earning criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.
Using a controversial move known as a “pocket rescission,” Trump said he wanted to nullify $810 million in spending that Congress had approved for programs and agencies, much of which would serve immigrants, minorities, and children.
Read More: A Debt Ceiling Fight Looms in 2027. Could a Democratic Congress Make it the Last One?
Over half of the cuts would land on the Health and Human Services (HHS) Department’s Office of Refugee Resettlement, according to a request sent to House Speaker Mike Johnson on Friday. It said that rescinding the funds is “consistent with the Administration's goal of ending the use of Federal taxpayer dollars to support non-citizens, putting Americans first.”
In a statement accompanying the request, the Trump Administration also called the funds “wasteful” and “harmful.”
The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan government watchdog, has asserted, however, that the move is an illegal sidestepping of the constitutionally protected separation of powers—chiefly, Congress's power of the purse.
A “pocket rescission” is not a formal or legal term; it was coined to reference a “ pocket veto ,” a process in which a bill fails to become law because the President does not sign it within 10 days and Congress’s adjournment prevents its return. Similarly, the “pocket rescission” aims to withdraw allocated funding without direct congressional intervention.
The timing is important when it comes to pocket rescissions. In order to be fully effective, this “occurs when a president asks Congress to rescind (or cancel) funds very close to the end of the fiscal year—so close that the funds expire before they can be used for new obligations,” according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO).
The Office of Management and Budget (OMB), helmed by Director Russell Vought, submitted the requests Friday and holds that the move is valid under the 1974 Impoundment Control Act (ICA).
The Impoundment Control Act was created in response to President Richard Nixon’s heavy use of impoundments to achieve his policy goals. It has since been used to limit or regulate a president’s ability to control spending that has already been appropriated by building in 45 days of continuous congressional session. During this time, Congress is meant to review a President’s rescission requests and either approve them or see the funds released as planned.
Trump’s request to cancel $810 million in funding, however, came just five days before the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30, all but ensuring that Congress will not have time to review the proposal in full or prevent the cuts from going into effect.
It is not the first time Trump has used this strategy to thwart spending attempts. He submitted a request on Aug. 28, 2025, to cancel $4.9 billion in foreign aid funds approved by Congress, including $3.2 billion that had been allocated to USAID . Although the move was contested, the Supreme Court last year stayed a lower court injunction requiring roughly $4 billion covered by the rescission request to be obligated.
The GAO claims that the move is illegal, writing on its website that this application of the ICA would “cede Congress’s power of the purse by allowing a president to, in effect, change the law by shortening the period of availability for fixed-period funds.”
“If Congress wanted a president to have that authority, it would need to change the law,” it continues.
Zachary Price, a professor at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco, says that the move is an “abuse” of the ICA.
“It’s perverse to read that as, instead, creating this mechanism for unilaterally canceling funds,” Price tells TIME, adding that this interpretation is not supported by a lot of “historical practice.”
The maneuver seeks to withhold the funds until they expire at the end of the fiscal year, leaving Congress little time to respond.
In this case, Price says, it further showcases how the ICA is being manipulated.
The government “shouldn't have a lot of money left over at the end of the fiscal year if you've been spending it as you go in the way the statute contemplates,” he says.
He also points out that the American government is distinctly separated into three branches, with Congress, sitting in the legislative branch, being given the power to pass legislation—or, in this case, cancel funds that have already been appropriated. It has been explicitly separated from the authority of the executive branch and the President.
Bobby Kogan, the senior director of federal budget policy at the Center for American Progress, says it even plainer than Price: “The administration has picked a bunch of things that they hate, and they say, ‘Well, we're just not going to do those.’”
The Supreme Court’s intervention last year did not constitute a ruling on the authority of pocket rescissions, meaning that the Trump Administration's latest use of the tactic could face new legal challenges.
The largest portion of this year’s proposed cuts will target HHS programs providing nonprofit services for refugees and unaccompanied minors. Trump’s request would withdraw $567 million from those services.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was also impacted, with a request to cancel funding for nonprofits that provide mental health services and social services to migrants. Another cut targets almost $25 million that had been slated for the Department of Education’s Special Programs for Migrant Students.
The Housing and Urban Development Department’s housing counseling services are also named amid the rescissions; the Trump Administration said that the program included non-governmental organizations with “divisive and DEI-centric agendas.”
The Trump Administration also aims to cancel $15 million from a Department of Justice office that focuses on reducing racial tensions, in addition to $10 million that had been allocated to the Minority Business Development Agency, which supports minority entrepreneurs.
“I assume that they're picking money to cancel based on some political calculus about what they can get away with,” Price says. When looking at the bigger picture, he argues this is just one maneuver in several to “establish stronger executive control over spending.”
The move also risks future negotiations in Congress, Price says. He explains that this application of the ICA would make it harder for Democrats and Republicans to compromise over spending if they anticipate that the sitting President will simply swoop in and cancel funding after thoughtful agreements have been reached.
“If the executive branch can come in and effectively impose a more kind of party line view of the spending, then you know why would people agree to the package in the first place?” he asks.
The rescission has earned blowback from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers who believe that the move sidesteps Congress's authority.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, lambasted the move on social media Friday evening , saying she would “work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions.”

articles.title_zh: US got pandas from China. Trump needs a lot more than that | Opinion
articles.content_orig:
While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “ stalemate summit ”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.
Instead, it was described as a celebration of “ diplotainment ” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.
One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.
To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.
With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.
That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.
On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”.
China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.”
Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.
On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.
For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely.
On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.”
For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

articles.title_orig: Recap: Iowa stuns Michigan on last-second touchdown pass
articles.title_zh: Recap: Iowa stuns Michigan on last-second touchdown pass
articles.content_orig:
Michigan got a taste of its own medicine on Saturday at the Big House.
The Wolverines, who were the beneficiaries of a controversial last-second win in their season opener, were victimized in the final plays of a devastating 20-19 loss to rival Iowa.
On the penultimate play of Iowa’s game-winning drive, Hawkeyes quarterback Hank Brown connected with receiver Addison Ostrenga to get into the red zone — but with just two seconds on the clock, time was going to run out before the offense could get another play off.
Unreal play to keep Iowa in it! pic.twitter.com/l6EY5M10t6
Then Iowa was handed a lifeline.
Michigan defensive end John Henry Daley went down with an injury during the play, meaning that the game clock halted at two seconds, giving Iowa another crack to score a game-winning touchdown.
And the Hawkeyes took full advantage, with Brown finding wideout Reece Vander Zee in the corner of the end zone for a 16-yard game-winning score.
The extra time on the clock comes with a bit of irony, as the Wolverines controversially defeated Western Michigan , 13-12, in their Week 1 win after officials awarded Michigan an extra second because a defender touched the ball with a second left on the stadium clock on the Wolverines’ initial Hail Mary attempt.
Given a second chance, Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood heaved a deep ball caught in the end zone by JJ Buchanan to seal the 13-12 win, which caused an uproar across college football.
On Saturday, however, it was Michigan on the receiving end as Iowa scored 13 unanswered points in the fourth quarter.
“One thing about these guys is that they don’t quit,” Hawkeyes head coach Kirk Ferentz said in a postgame interview. “It wasn’t perfect, but they don’t give up.”
The win is Iowa’s first victory over a ranked Big Ten opponent since 2021, snapping a nine-game losing streak against such teams.
“Never won like this, so it’s what we’ll all remember,” Ferentz added.
“We’ll enjoy the heck out of it tonight, and back to work tomorrow.”

articles.title_orig: OpenAI pauses training of latest models after agents probed US government sites in unexpected ways
articles.title_zh: OpenAI pauses training of latest models after agents probed US government sites in unexpected ways
articles.content_orig:
Decision follows disclosures that OpenAI agents searching government websites had acted in unexpected ways
OpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount.
The decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.
Separately, the AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a US Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.
OpenAI said in a statement that it will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expects it will have to “hit pause” again as AI develops and other issues emerge.
AI labs are facing pressure from lawmakers and tech experts to slow development so they can build guardrails to stop agents from acting on their own, hacking websites and disclosing nonpublic information. The heads of both OpenAI and rival Anthropic have called for a slowdown too.
It is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first came in July after disclosure of a cyber-attack targeting AI startup Hugging Face , a now notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.
In a meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping this week, Donald Trump agreed to share information on AI dangers and coordinate efforts to keep it safe. Trump believes AI fears are overblown, though, and later suggested that he plans no crackdown of his own.
The US is not going to be “putting on brakes”, Trump told reporters outside the White House. “They want to stop our progress because we’re leading China by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.”
The latest OpenAI incidents did not appear to involve the disclosure of any nonpublic information but were concerning enough for the company to warn the federal agencies involved.
In the education department incident, OpenAI agents found API “developer keys” to access government data, though ultimately only publicly available information was gathered.
In another case involving the securities and exchange commission, agents found information freely available to all but then posted it elsewhere on the internet, an act that went beyond what they were instructed to do.
US Securities and Exchange Commission spokesperson Kurt Hopfenspirger said on Saturday that “no nonpublic information was accessed”.
The Department of Education said earlier that it found “no evidence of any impact to our website or databases”.
Several other AI companies have disclosed incidents of their models going rogue and even hacking websites.
OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, said in a social media post on Friday that the Hugging Face incident “is still the most severe event we’ve seen”.
OpenAI previously shared six other reports of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances.

articles.title_orig: As Hurricane Nolo stalls near Hawaii’s Big Island, serious flooding likely
articles.title_zh: As Hurricane Nolo stalls near Hawaii’s Big Island, serious flooding likely
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Nolo weakened slightly to a Category 1 storm Saturday as it began to move away from Hawaii, the National Hurricane Center said , but it was still expected to lash Hawaii's Big Island and Maui with heavy rains through the weekend.
The storm was inching west late Saturday morning local time at just 5 mph, the NHC said. It was forecast to remain well south of Hawaii's two big islands, although it was expected to strengthen into a major hurricane on Sunday and Monday before weakening next week.
President Trump on Friday approved an emergency declaration for Hawaii that will provide federal resources and assistance to the state in its recovery from Nolo, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said.
Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 90 mph, making it a Category 1 hurricane. This comes after it had strengthened Friday into a Category 2 storm with 105-mph winds. The hurricane center, however, said it would likely re-strengthen Sunday and become a major hurricane, which is defined as a Category 3 storm or stronger.
Hurricane-force winds were extending outward up to 35 miles from Nolo's core and tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 150 miles.
A tropical storm warning was in effect for Hawaii County — the Big Island — which could see over two feet of rain. Catastrophic and life-threatening flash flooding is possible on the Big Island through the weekend, forecasters warned. A hurricane watch for the island was canceled.
A tropical storm watch was in effect for Maui County.
Nolo could bring up to 25 inches of rain to the eastern and southern portions of the Big Island, forecasters said, and the island's western areas could see 1 to 2 inches of rain. For Maui, 4 to 8 inches is possible. The rest of Hawaii is likely to get 1 to 3 inches, with 5 at most, enough to trigger isolated flooding, forecasters said.
All state parks on the Big Island and on Maui will be closed because of the storm, the state's Department of Land and Natural Resources said.
Nolo formed as another storm, Hurricane Polo , continued to swirl in the Pacific, off Mexico's southwestern coast.
The latest storms add to an unusually active season in the Pacific. Earlier this month, Hurricane Lowell brought damaging winds and heavy rain to the western Hawaiian islands of Kauai and Niihau, bringing down trees, damaging roads and knocking out power for thousands.
Last month, Hurricane Lala washed away about 100 homes , triggered landslides and caused widespread power outages as it brushed past Hawaii.

KNOXVILLE, Tenn. — Colin Simmons tied the program record with five sacks as top-ranked Texas held off No. 14 Tennessee 20-17 Saturday with President Donald Trump on hand in the Longhorns’ first visit to Neyland Stadium.
Raleek Brown ran for 67 yards and a pair of touchdowns, and his 4-yarder with 5:41 left gave the Longhorns the winning margin in the Southeastern Conference opener for both teams. Giannis Spetic had a pair of field goals.
It was a defensive day with Texas (4-0) dominating with 10 sacks, led by Simmons. The linebacker’s day for the record books also will be remembered for his vulgar celebration after one sack. He was flagged for unsportsmanlike conduct with the referee saying Simmons was “simulating” using the restroom.
Tennessee quarterback Brandon Faizon made it interesting late, capping an 80-yard drive with a 30-yard TD pass to Mike Matthews with 1:22 left. Linebacker Arion Carter recovered the onside kick, and Jelani McDonald batted away Brandon’s pass to Travis Smith Jr. on the final play in the end zone.
NO. 2 GEORGIA 41, OKLAHOMA 13
ATHENS, Ga. — Chris Cole scored on a 85-yard fumble return as Georgia took advantage of three first-half turnovers by John Mateer and overwhelmed struggling Oklahoma.
Mateer lost two fumbles, each recovered by Cole, and threw an interception in the first half as Oklahoma (2-2, 0-1 Southeastern Conference) fell behind 28-0. K.J. Bolden picked off a pass from Mateer in the second quarter.
While Mateer struggled with turnovers, Gunner Stockton was almost perfect in the first half for Georgia (4-0, 2-0). Stockton completed his first nine passes, including a 35-yard touchdown throw to Talyn Taylor.
The Sooners finished with four turnovers, including a fumble by tight end Rocky Beers in the third quarter.
Mateer’s second lost fumble, forced by Raylen Wilson, was returned 23 yards by Cole late in the first half to set up Chauncey Bowens’ second touchdown run.
Georgia rolled despite holding out its top running back, Nate Frazier, due to injured ribs. Bowens had touchdown runs of 2 and 6 yards as the fill-in starter. Dwight Phillips added a 54-yard touchdown run early in the fourth quarter.
NO. 3 NOTRE DAME 49, PURDUE 10
WEST LAFAYETTE, Ind. — CJ Carr threw three touchdown passes and ran for another score, linebacker Drayk Bowen scored his first career TD on a 15-yard fumble return and Notre Dame beat Purdue.
Carr was 14 of 22 for 237 yards and threw his first interception of the season. It’s the second straight week Carr has had a TD pass and a TD run in the same game. Aneyas Williams carried 14 times for 80 yards with one TD as the Fighting Irish (4-0) produced a season-high 177 yards rushing.
Notre Dame has won 14 straight and will start October with a perfect record for the first time since 2021.
It was another miserable day for the struggling Boilermakers (1-3). Ryan Browne was 18 of 28 for 111 yards and lost the fumble that Bowen returned for the touchdown. Purdue had only 12 yards rushing in the first half and finished the game with only 218 total yards as it lost its third straight.
NO. 21 FLORIDA 52, NO. 4 MISSISSIPPI 28
GAINESVILLE, Fla. — Jadan Baugh ran for 142 yards and three touchdowns, Duke Clark added 126 yards and a score on the ground, and Florida manhandled Mississippi to reach 4-0 for the first time since 2019.
The Gators (4-0, 2-0 Southeastern Conference), installed as 3 1/2-point favorites, proved Las Vegas oddsmakers right by leading from start to finish. They scored touchdowns on five consecutive drives in the second half.
The Rebels (3-1, 1-1) insisted that last week’s victory against LSU, the one that spoiled former Ole Miss coach Lane Kiffin’s return, was not their “Super Bowl.” But they failed to build off that emotional win.
Florida had a lot to do with it.
The Gators jumped on the Rebels early, leading 10-0 before Heisman Trophy front-runner Trinidad Chambliss even threw a pass, and set the pace the rest of the afternoon. Florida was unstoppable running the ball.
NO. 7 OHIO ST. 42, ILLINOIS 19
COLUMBUS, Ohio — Jeremiah Smith tied an Ohio State record with four touchdown catches and also had career highs with 12 receptions for 217 yards as the Buckeyes beat Illinois.
According to Sportradar, it is the 23rd time since 2000 a FBS player has had double-digit catches for at least 200 yards and four scores in a game. The last to do it was Western Michigan’s Sky Moore against Northern Illinois in 2021.
It is the fifth time an Ohio State receiver has had four touchdowns. The last time it happened before Saturday was Noah Brown at Oklahoma in 2016.
It also tied for the sixth-most receiving yards in an OSU game and tied for sixth-most receptions.
Smith tied the mark with 10:07 remaining in the fourth quarter when he was wide open on a 26-yard touchdown to extend the Buckeyes’ lead to 35-13.
Smith also became the third receiver since 2015 from a Power Four conference to have at least three games with at least 150 receiving yards and two touchdowns in one half. DeVonta Smith had four at Alabama and Ja’Marr Chase did it three times at LSU.
NO. 11 TEXAS TECH 49, SAM HOUSTON 14
LUBBOCK, Texas — Texas Tech linebacker Austin Romaine became the first FBS player in 13 years to return two interceptions for touchdowns on consecutive throws, Cameron Dickey ran for two scores and the Red Raiders beat Sam Houston.
Both pick-6s by Romaine came in the opening minute of the second quarter, and were against different quarterbacks.
The Red Raiders (4-0) extended their home winning streak to 11 games, their longest since 12 in a row from 2007-09.
A nearly five TD favorite, Texas Tech led only 21-14 at halftime before Dickey’s second scoring run, a 13-yarder, and Will Hammond’s 21-yard TD to Coy Eakin in the first five minutes after the break.
Hammond finished 17-of-29 passing for 224 yards, but threw three interceptions in the final 5 1/2 minutes of the first half — though Sam Houston (1-3) got only seven points off those. Hammond added a 23-yard TD run in the fourth quarter.

Parker rushed for a career-high 174 yards and two TDs on 18 carries and caught five passes for 65 yards and a score for the Utes (4-0, 1-0 Big 12).

articles.content_orig:
Michigan got a taste of its own medicine on Saturday at the Big House.
The Wolverines, who were the beneficiaries of a controversial last-second win in their season opener, were victimized in the final plays of a devastating 20-19 loss to rival Iowa.
On the penultimate play of Iowa’s game-winning drive, Hawkeyes quarterback Hank Brown connected with receiver Addison Ostrenga to get into the red zone — but with just two seconds on the clock, time was going to run out before the offense could get another play off.
Unreal play to keep Iowa in it! pic.twitter.com/l6EY5M10t6
Then Iowa was handed a lifeline.
Michigan defensive end John Henry Daley went down with an injury during the play, meaning that the game clock halted at two seconds, giving Iowa another crack to score a game-winning touchdown.
And the Hawkeyes took full advantage, with Brown finding wideout Reece Vander Zee in the corner of the end zone for a 16-yard game-winning score.
The extra time on the clock comes with a bit of irony, as the Wolverines controversially defeated Western Michigan , 13-12, in their Week 1 win after officials awarded Michigan an extra second because a defender touched the ball with a second left on the stadium clock on the Wolverines’ initial Hail Mary attempt.
Given a second chance, Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood heaved a deep ball caught in the end zone by JJ Buchanan to seal the 13-12 win, which caused an uproar across college football.
On Saturday, however, it was Michigan on the receiving end as Iowa scored 13 unanswered points in the fourth quarter.
“One thing about these guys is that they don’t quit,” Hawkeyes head coach Kirk Ferentz said in a postgame interview. “It wasn’t perfect, but they don’t give up.”
The win is Iowa’s first victory over a ranked Big Ten opponent since 2021, snapping a nine-game losing streak against such teams.
“Never won like this, so it’s what we’ll all remember,” Ferentz added.
“We’ll enjoy the heck out of it tonight, and back to work tomorrow.”

articles.title_zh: NFL says Maracanã Stadium field passed required tests before Cowboys-Ravens kickoff
articles.content_orig:
The playing surface at Brazil's Maracanã Stadium passed all testing Friday following concerns voiced by the NFL Players Association.
NFL field director Nick Pappas met with reporters on Saturday, one day before the Baltimore Ravens and Dallas Cowboys are set to play . Pappas said that all mandatory requirements have been met regarding the surface, and testing was done in conjunction with the NFLPA and an independent specialist.
"We have an independent inspector that comes in, walks with myself, walks with a member of the NFLPA," Pappas said. "They were here yesterday. Performed that test. Things check out. We've made additional improvements to the field that we think were helpful."
However, close-up footage taken by Dallas' 105.3 The Fan showed several very thin patches on the field with sparse tufts of grass sprouting up from green-colored dirt.
Pappas added that the league has visited the stadium once a month since January for regular checkups. The region has seen a lot of rainfall of late, plus games played by soccer clubs Flamengo and Fluminense, including one last Sunday.
"I mean rest was No. 1, right?" Pappas said about the work that's been done since last weekend. "Giving the opportunity to get some rest, made a phone call to shut the rain off. So we've got some sunshine now. I wish I could take credit for that. Stitching was a big piece of it, but then also bringing in the field goal posts, getting the lines and getting things measured out and laid out. There's got to be a football field out here too."
On Friday, NFLPA executive director JC Tretter posted a lengthy statement on social media , including what has needed to be addressed with the grass playing surface in Rio de Janeiro leading up to kickoff on Sunday.
"The concern heading into this week was that the field would be loose, patchy, and lead to excessive slipping," Tretter wrote. "Those conditions are generally more of a playability and performance issue than a significant injury concern."
Tretter added that safety is the primary issue for players. But a surface that allows them to perform at their highest level, resulting in a well-played game, is also a major consideration.
Both the league and experts hired by the NFLPA have checked the field during the past week and found that the grass surface wasn't stable enough to be suitable for a game. The latest assessment means they will definitely play football there on Sunday.
The Cowboys arrived at the stadium on Saturday for a walkthrough to test out the surface. Some players, like CeeDee Lamb , went barefoot . Others, like kicker Brandon Aubrey , wore cleats to get a better idea of how the footing will hold up.
Kickoff is scheduled for 4:25 p.m. ET on Sunday with the Cowboys serving as the home team.

Tesla Supercharger StationTesla Model Y electric vehicle connected to a Tesla Supercharger in a shopping center parking lot, Walnut Creek, California, September 14, 2026. (Photo by Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump has signed off on new fuel economy standards that he claims will end a Biden-era push for carmakers to build more electric vehicles.
On Monday, the U.S. Department of Transportation is expected to approve new, dramatically reduced emissions standards that will last through 2031. In a post announcing his support for the move, Trump said "these new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America."
"That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car – Far better than the Environmental Monsters that we were building heretofore," Trump wrote in his post. "Every Manufacturer, from General Motors to Ford Stellantis, has called me wanting to build here, and now they can!"
Trump blasted the current fuel economy standards, arguing that they cost manufacturers billions of dollars, wasted billions on chargers, and forced people to buy vehicles that they did not want.
The new standards are expected to cut the cost of building new vehicles, but will drive up fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emissions for decades, the U.S. Department of Transportation predicts.
RELATED: Trump rescinds nearly $1B in funds approved by Congress: Why senators say it's illegal
According to Reuters , the new proposal would require an automaker’s fleetwide fuel economy average to be 34.5 miles per gallon by 2031, a sharp decrease from the 50.4 miles per gallon under the current regulations.
Reducing the restrictions is predicted to shave $930 off the cost of an average new vehicle, Reuters reported. Conversely, the new standards are expected to result in 100 billion more gallons of fuel to be consumed, an extra $185 billion spent on fuel, and an increase in carbon dioxide emissions by 5%, according to DOT numbers.
Reuters quoted former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who led the agency under President Joe Biden, as saying "lowering standards will accelerate what (Trump) has already been doing: handing the clean tech future to China and forcing Americans to pay more at the pump."

SEAL BEACH, Calif. (KABC) -- If you are thinking about heading to the beach, you might want to reconsider -- along with big waves, Hurricane Polo could bring dangerous rip currents, flooding and more erosion to Southern California.
High sand berms line up the shoreline, protecting homes in Seal Beach as residents there prepare for another storm heading their way.
Although SoCal shores will not get hit directly by Hurricane Polo, heading towards Mexico, its impact will still be felt in our region, especially at south-facing beaches. Those areas could see waves up to 7 feet tall or higher in the coming days.
Flooding, high surf and dangerous rip currents are expected, along with seeing more beach erosion.
Residents preparing for the upcoming storm are hoping the built-up sand berms and other preparations make a difference this time around.
"I think they're gonna hold, because we weren't  prepared, I don't think Seal Beach was prepared for the last one," said area resident Susana Villalon.
"If you go down to Aliso Creek Beach, you can see how much the sand disappeared," said Laguna Beach resident Trish Sweeney. "And we lost quit a bit of sand over the years...shown how much damage it is."
The peninsula in Long Beach, another community hit hard by the effects of Hurricane Marie over Labor Day weekend, has been closed for public safety and residents were urged to stay off sand berms and avoid areas where heavy equipment is operating.
City officials were urging residents to prepare for high tides, large swells and possible coastal flooding from swells generated by Hurricane Polo, with the greatest flooding risk expected Monday and Tuesday.
The Long Beach City Council ratified a proclamation of a local emergency so they can activate the resources they need to head ahead of this storm.
Local fire departments are also on high alert. Ready-to-fill sandbags are available at all Los Angeles Fire Department neighborhood fire stations -- up to 25 bags per household.
A beach hazard statement is going to be in effect through Wednesday.
City News Service contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Windy weddings and rocky cruises: How East Coasters are braving the nor'easter this weekend
articles.title_zh: Windy weddings and rocky cruises: How East Coasters are braving the nor'easter this weekend
articles.content_orig:
John Garrisi, left, and Gaige Graf move an outdoor table away from the shorefront during the early stages of a nor'easter storm on Friday. Robert F. Bukaty/AP hide caption
Talia Manno opened her door on Saturday morning to waves lapping halfway up the front steps to her Atlantic City, N.J., home.
"It got up to my fifth step," Manno said. "I was really freaking out."
Manno, a lifelong resident, said the last time water came that high was during Hurricane Sandy .
"Even if you live here and you see high tide and flooding, that was really scary and it happened so fast," she said.
Manno is among tens of millions of people from the mid-Atlantic through the coast of Maine who are in the path of a powerful and rare September nor'easter that is bringing coastal flooding, heavy rain and high winds this weekend.
Nearly 80,000 people were without power across New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Connecticut and Massachusetts, as of Saturday evening, according to the PowerOutage.com map. The storm is expected to continue hitting the Jersey Shore, New York City, and Eastern Massachusetts into Sunday, according to NWS.
Videos posted on social media Saturday showed streets inundated with water in New Jersey, and massive waves hitting the coast . In New York City, people were seen kayaking in the streets . New Jersey and New York declared states of emergency in counties across the two states, including in New York City.
Francis Tarasiewicz, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Massachusetts, said wind gusts along the coast could reach up to 60 miles per hour this weekend. This nor'easter comes earlier than the typical October through May storm season, he said, and will last longer than normal.
Spectators watch wave break during a nor'easter storm on Saturday in Hampton, N.H. Robert F. Bukat/AP hide caption
"Many nor'easters affect the area over the course of about a day," he said. "It's a quick punch of strong winds, in many cases, heavy snow or rain." But, Tarasiewicz said, "with this one, we're looking at about a 48-hour period of winds greater than 35 to 40 miles per hour across the area."
The nor'easter is also making travel difficult. More than 1,000 flights were canceled Saturday with thousands more delayed, according to data from FlightAware . Ferry services on Cape Cod and in Rhode Island were disrupted, and Amtrak canceled several trains due to the weather and downed wires.
Off the coast of New York, the strong winds made for a rough cruise ride for Jessica Lisboa. She brought green apples, ginger ale and an acupressure anti-nausea bracelet to prepare for the Bermuda-bound cruise.
"Let me not sugarcoat it. Was it wild? Yeah, sure. It was a little wild," Lisboa said. "It felt honestly like a roller coaster." Still, she considered it a worthwhile adventure.
The nor'easter also took out a number of events planned for the weekend. Oceans Calling, one of Maryland's biggest music festivals, was canceled on Friday. An AC/DC concert in New Jersey was rescheduled. The Boston Red Sox announced they would move their game against the Chicago Cubs.
Some East Coasters found a way to adapt.
When Olga Ostrovetsky picked a date in September for her small outdoor wedding, she envisioned a beautiful, fall day.
But as she got ready to tie the knot in Wallkill, N.Y., she said, "It's very, very windy."
At first bummed, she's now finding the positives in the disruption.
"It's kind of fitting, to be honest, because my fiancé and I met and it was a torrential downpour," she said. "We met on a day like this, and we're also getting married on a day like this," she said.
As for Manno, the Atlantic City resident, is planning to spend Saturday night with family away from the coast. After this nor'easter, she said she doesn't know how much longer she'll live in the area.
"As the years pass, it seems like it's just getting more and more flooding," she said. "It's crazy."

Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi called at the United Nations Saturday for "self-restraint" from all sides in the Middle East war, while stressing that Muscat was ready to mediate.
"We call upon all parties concerned to settle their outstanding disputes through pursuing a policy of self-restraint and foresight, and through engaging in dialog to reach consensual, political solutions and sustainable understandings for the benefit of all," Albusaidi said, addressing world leaders gathered in New York.
"Oman once again reaffirms its steadfast commitment to continuing its efforts aimed at safeguarding navigation in the Strait of Hormuz ... We also call upon all parties to cooperate with Oman in these efforts."
Oman sits across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, and ships seeking to skirt Tehran's restrictions have recently been taking a route that hugs the Omani coast.
Saudi Arabia warned U.N. members Saturday that attempts to block Middle East waterways are a threat to global energy security and demanded the international community do more to defend freedom of navigation.
"The international community has been absent from assuming its responsibilities in confronting all that threatens international peace and security," Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan told the United Nations General Assembly.
"The kingdom stresses the importance of guaranteeing the protection of freedom of navigation in all international waterways, foremost among them the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden," he said.
The minister further demanded the return of conditions in the Strait of Hormuz to what they were before Feb. 28, without imposing any fees or taxes.
"The kingdom rejects any party's use of these vital passages as a tool for pressure, threat, or harm to the interests of states, in a manner consistent with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions," he said.
Bin Farhan was speaking shortly after President Trump had rejected an Iranian proposal of a deal to reopen Hormuz, in exchange for — among other conditions — a Middle East ceasefire and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
Reopening the Strait of Hormuz has been the focal point of much of the negotiations, but the Saudis have been facing increased difficulties transporting oil due to the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen effectively closing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern exit to the Red Sea, through targeting Saudi-flagged tankers and attacks on the East-West pipeline through inland Saudi Arabia.
As the world deals with decreasing oil supplies and increasing prices, President Trump asked his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to increase petroleum production in his country, according to the White House.
The White House provided a fact sheet following Mr. Trump's meeting with Xi for a state visit this week that highlights "President Trump urged President Xi to increase production of refined petroleum products to stabilize global supply."
The war with Iran, and its spread to Saudi Arabia, has tightened global energy supplies even as the U.S. has worked to escort tankers out of the Persian Gulf. Mr. Trump said earlier Saturday that 29 vessels had been guided out of the Strait of Hormuz under military supervision.
But the supply of oil and natural gas have still suffered compared to prewar levels. And the revived fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government has now led to the closure of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Saudi-flagged oil tankers.
Brent crude, the international standard, closed the week at $104 a barrel, the same as it began the week, despite rising to $108 on Thursday.
Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Russia is ready to help stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region, as the U.S.-Iran conflict drags on.
"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov told leaders Saturday at the U.N. General Assembly.
"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region."
Lavrov did not elaborate on how Russia would provide assistance to end the conflict spreading across the Middle East.
Russia has long been an ally of Iran. Iran provided Shahed drones to Russia for its own invasion of Ukraine. Russia in turn has reportedly assisted Iran with satellite coordination to target U.S. forces in the region.
The Israeli army destroyed an alleged Hezbollah weapons storage facility in southern Lebanon on Saturday.
"Earlier today (Saturday), the IDF struck a weapons storage facility belonging to the Hezbollah terrorist organization in the Sejoud area of southern Lebanon," the IDF said in a statement. "The strike was carried out to remove a threat: the facility stored weapons that were used to target IDF soldiers operating in the Security Zone."
The so-called "security zone" is an area of southern Lebanon set up by Israel that reaches about 6 or 7 miles into the country from the northern Israeli border.
Israel and Hezbollah have signed several short-term ceasefires, mostly recently in late June, but they have all been punctuated by violations from both sides. Deals signed between Israel and the Lebanese government, including the trilateral agreement brokered by the U.S., have each been rejected by Hezbollah.
President Trump has rejected the latest proposal from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in seven days and launch in-depth negotiations to end the war.
"I'm rejecting their deal," Mr. Trump told reporters while leaving the White House on Saturday to travel to Tennessee. "They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they are losing so badly. You don't see that in the fake news. We're winning tremendously, we have total control of the Hormuz Strait, massive amounts of oil are coming out of the Hormuz Strait, last night we had 29 ships come out."
"They want to make a deal," he continued. "I think that's fine, I like making a deal too. But that deal [they offered] would not be acceptable."
Both the U.S. and Iran had expressed optimism over talks held in New York during the U.N. General Assembly, though they were short on details of what was discussed. Mr. Trump did not attend the talks directly, but his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and special envoy Steve Witkoff were involved in the negotiations with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz was reportedly similar to the Islamabad memorandum signed in June, including ending the blockade, allowing Iranian oil sales and halting fighting in every Middle East theater. The U.S. disputed Iran's interpretation of the MOU over who controlled traffic in the strait and the deal fell apart by July.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had told CBS News' Margaret Brennan on Friday that his country was standing at the ready to implement the new deal.
"If this message reaches the president of the United States, or the interviewers and those involved in the discussions, naturally the process will begin from the very day they accept it," he said.
China pushed back against the United States in its speech at the U.N. General Assembly on Saturday, saying sovereignty of countries in the Gulf should be respected.
Vice President Han Zheng did not mention the U.S. by name in his remarks.
The comments stood in sharp contrast to the friendship on display earlier this week at the White House, where President Trump feted Chinese leader Xi Jinping with military flyovers and at a lavish state dinner.
"Major countries should have special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security, and they should take the lead in complying with the rules, upholding rule of law, and doing what's right," Han said.
"China holds that the sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East, including the Gulf, should be respected," he added.

articles.title_zh: Trump says he approved new fuel economy standards ending Biden-era electric vehicle mandate
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Saturday said he approved new fuel economy standards , reversing former President Joe Biden's stricter policies meant to fuel electric vehicle adoption.
Since the Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, standards were established in 1975, they have been periodically updated, typically to make vehicles more efficient. Under former President Joe Biden's standards , automakers would have had to increase the fuel efficiency of their passenger cars and light trucks to roughly 50 miles per gallon by 2031. The stricter standards were designed to incentivize electric vehicle production and sales in the U.S.
Trump presented the policy change as a boon for both automakers and consumers, though the final standards have not yet been publicly detailed.
"These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car — Far better than the Environmental Monsters that we were building heretofore," he wrote in the Truth Social post . "Every Manufacturer, from General Motors to Ford to Stellantis, has called me wanting to build here, and now they can!"
The regulatory change would fulfill a campaign promise from Trump to rescind policies that encouraged or incentivized electric vehicles.
It is unclear what the final fuel economy standards will be, although Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy previously said that they would be sharply lower than the Biden-era policies.
Weaker fuel economy standards mean that automakers can produce more pickup trucks and SUVs, which are much more profitable than smaller cars but have worse gas mileage. Electric vehicles also become much less attractive to automakers, although some companies, like General Motors , have said that they will still make them.

articles.content_orig:
Tennessee Volunteers fans told OutKick's Trey Wallace they're excited for President Donald Trump to attend a key SEC matchup against the Texas Longhorns on Saturday, and they left with their final score predictions.
KNOXVILLE, TN - Cigar smoke was coming from the Texas locker room following their win over Tennessee on Saturday afternoon that came down to the final play.
The only offense that we really got on a consistent basis Saturday between Tennessee and Texas came when the Secret Service was clearing an area for President Trump to walk through while the national anthem was being played.
A slugfest of wacky proportions played out inside Neyland Stadium, with Arch Manning doing just enough to get his Longhorns out of Knoxville with the win.
SEC CROWD GREETS TRUMP WITH MASSIVE CHEERS AHEAD OF TENNESSEE-TEXAS SHOWDOWN
The entire morning was filled with anticipation, as the President would finally make his way from the airport to Tennessee's campus for what would turn out to be a first half appearance.
But, it was the Texas defense that showed up for the party with a reckoning on its mind, finishing with ten total sacks, which Steve Sarkisian said led to eight Tennessee players being helped out of the field in what turned out to be another physical SEC game.
TENNESSEE FANS EXCITED FOR TRUMP'S ATTENDANCE AT GAME VS TEXAS: 'I HOPE HE STAYS THE WHOLE GAME'
What's the biggest takeaway?
Texas QB Arch Manning talks about the Longhorns win over Tennessee (Via: Trey Wallace. OutKick)
The Longhorns have the two-best wins in college football this season, after defeating Ohio State just fourteen days ago.
Steve Sarkisian, will not apologize for how his team wins, nor should he.
"For us, we’ve got more of these to go..We have 7 ranked opponents we have still yet to play..That's why I’m not gonna apologize for how we beat a top-15 team on the road, when others don’t even play them," Sarkisian said postgame.
Head Coach Steve Sarkisian of the Texas Longhorns looks on during the first half against the Tennessee Volunteers at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville, Tenn., on Sept. 26, 2026. (Getty Images)
We wondered how the Longhorns would react to a hostile environment, with over 100,000 fans starting to enter the gates in hopes of taking advantage of alcoholic beverages that were 50% off , thanks to the Tennessee athletic department enticing fans to enter the stadium before traffic got out of hand due to Trump's arrival.
That answer was provided on the defensive side of the ball for Texas throughout the entire game, as Tennessee quarterback Faizon Brandon scrambled for his life on what felt like every other play for the Vols.
DONALD TRUMP ADDS POLITICAL STAKES, ANTICIPATION AND POTENTIAL SIDELINE CHAOS TO TEXAS-TENNESSEE SHOWDOWN
Heck, Texas' Colin Simmons had five sacks on the day, making life extremely difficult for the Vols freshman QB.
If you were under the impression that this Steve Sarkisian led football team wasn’t prepared for their first road trip of the season, you were sorely mistaken. There were some that wrote about how this physical test on the road would be to their detriment.
NO. 1 TEXAS ESCAPES TENNESSEE WITH THRILLING SEC VICTORY AS PRESIDENT TRUMP WATCHES ON FROM NEYLAND STADIUM
I guess they aren't watching the same Texas team. This group continues to find ways to win, in the most difficult era of college football. Whether it was on the final play of the game, or holding off an offense on the last series, the Longhorns have figured it out early this season.
Sure, he might have only thrown for 127 yards in the first half, taking a 10-3 lead into halftime. But, that didn’t stop him from finding pockets of success in the second half, which kept his team ahead when the final whistle blew.
And yes, Manning only finished the game with 201 yards passing with zero touchdowns, but he put Texas in a position to win once again.
Whether it was Cam Coleman or Ryan Wingo, Tennessee did not seem to have an answer for the talented pair on a consistent basis, which came back to bite the Vols during the second half.
Seven total sacks for the Texas defense also kept the Vols offense in check for a majority of the game.
This was the first road test, and they passed. At the end of the day, when Texas boards the plane home for Austin, that's all that matters for this team.
We can talk about some of the sloppy offensive line play, or the weird unsportsmanlike penalty on Colin Simmons, but that's just noise right now.
What we witnessed on Saturday afternoon was two teams who are still working out the glitches. The problem for Tennessee is that they do not have a veteran starter, while Arch Manning is finding different ways to get his squad into the end zone.
KNOXVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 26: Arch Manning #16 of the Texas Longhorns carries the ball during a game between the Tennessee Volunteers and the Texas Longhorns at Neyland Stadium on September 26, 2026 in Knoxville, Tennessee. (Photo by Roger Wimmer/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) ( )
All the while, Texas once again proved they might be the best overall team in college football in one of the hardest places to play in this sport.
As the equipment staff began loading the truck for its ride back to Texas, you can hear the noise coming from inside the Longhorns locker room.
"We're the real UT, so they can stop talking," one player said aloud.
On Saturday afternoon in Knoxville, this Texas team once again proved it could find another way to win.
But, in the end, it still came down to their defense. Just as it did against Ohio State.
You don't rack up 12 sacks on an SEC opponent without having a stellar group on that side of the ball. Maybe we should be talking more about the unit who has provided four wins on the season, with two against Top-15 teams.

President Donald Trump told a female reporter to be “quiet” in his latest tense exchange with the press , then separately dismissed the idea that women govern better than men as “ridiculous.”
The 80-year-old president made the remarks Saturday while speaking with reporters outside the White House before departing for a college football game in Tennessee .
A female journalist asked Trump whether he wanted only outlets that “support” him included in the White House press pool after he banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House last week. A federal judge blocked that decision Thursday but Trump barred CNN from Air Force One Saturday and replaced the outlet with LindellTV .
“No, no,” Trump responded. “I want real news, not fake news like you. Listen, I want real news. I love an open free press. What I don’t like is the fake press.”
Trump went on to claim that CNN and MS NOW had low ratings. When the same reporter, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner , followed up by asking: “Do you not want tough questions?” Trump cut her off.
“Wait wait, quiet,” Trump said, raising his index finger. “What I don't like is fake news. And they’re fake news.”
Trump has long had a combative relationship with the press , accusing reporters of biased and unfair coverage. He has also directed personal insults at journalists and suggesting that some should face punishment.
His attacks have often been aimed at female reporters. In June, he lashed out at CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins , saying she had “hatred in her eyes” and that “I never see a smile.” He had earlier called Collins “stupid and nasty” after she questioned him about the White House ballroom.
Last November, Trump told a female Bloomberg journalist, “ Quiet, piggy ,” when she tried to ask about Jeffrey Epstein . The White House responded to that remark by saying Trump is “very frank and honest with everyone.”
Trump was also asked Saturday morning about comments former President Barack Obama made this week about women in government.
“If you put women in charge of every government for like two years and then just kind of saw alright how are things going, I have a strong belief that things would — they wouldn’t be perfect — but they’d be better,” Obama had said Monday.
“It's ridiculous,” Trump opined. “I love women. I think they're great. But what a ridiculous statement that is.”
Trump also addressed a number of other issues. He said the United States would not put “brakes” on artificial intelligence development, which he again described as “super intelligence.”
He separately urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to “make a deal” to end Russia’s war in Ukraine and claimed that the U.S. has “total control” of the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he approved new fuel economy standards rolling back Biden-era rules
articles.title_zh: Trump says he approved new fuel economy standards rolling back Biden-era rules
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Saturday said he approved new fuel economy standards , reversing former President Joe Biden's stricter policies meant to fuel electric vehicle adoption.
Since the Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, standards were established in 1975, they have been periodically updated, typically to make vehicles more efficient. Under former President Joe Biden's standards , automakers would have had to increase the fuel efficiency of their passenger cars and light trucks to roughly 50 miles per gallon by 2031. The stricter standards were designed to incentivize electric vehicle production and sales in the U.S.
Trump presented the policy change as a boon for both automakers and consumers, though the final standards have not yet been publicly detailed.
"These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car — Far better than the Environmental Monsters that we were building heretofore," he wrote in the Truth Social post . "Every Manufacturer, from General Motors to Ford to Stellantis, has called me wanting to build here, and now they can!"
The regulatory change would fulfill a campaign promise from Trump to rescind policies that encouraged or incentivized electric vehicles.
It is unclear what the final fuel economy standards will be, although Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy previously said that they would be sharply lower than the Biden-era policies.
Weaker fuel economy standards mean that automakers can produce more pickup trucks and SUVs, which are much more profitable than smaller cars but have worse gas mileage. Electric vehicles also become much less attractive to automakers, although some companies, like General Motors , have said that they will still make them.

Boeing said it flagged a software glitch last month on some 737 Max aircraft that could affect certain landing procedures, as the manufacturer seeks federal approval for the fourth and final model in its best-selling aircraft family.
The Federal Aviation Administration said Saturday that it is assessing the problem and "will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern" and that it will review Boeing's proposed fix.
Boeing said the issue could arise after a missed approach when pilots alter a preprogrammed flight path, and that pilots must take additional steps to use automated tools on subsequent approaches.
"We shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases. Our engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue," Boeing said. The Wall Street Journal reported the issue earlier.
The company said that pilots are trained to land without the automated system. "We are working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur," Boeing said.
U.S. airlines told CNBC that they do not have Max 8 and Max 9 airplanes with the updated software tied to the glitch in their fleets. Airlines can revert some Maxes to the older software version.
All-Boeing 737 Max carrier Southwest Airlines said it is "aware of the issue and is engaged with Boeing and the FAA."
It added that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes." United Airlines also said it's not taking any Max aircraft deliveries with the new software.
However, questions remain about the two other models, the Max 7 and Max 10. The Federal Aviation Administration certified the Max 7 , the smallest of the Max family, in early August with the newest software installed. It wasn't immediately clear if the aircraft could be delivered or fly with an older version of software.
Additionally, Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors earlier this month that he expected FAA certification of the Max 10 "very soon."
"We have been engaged with Boeing and the FAA and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps," Alaska Airlines , a Max 10 customer, said Saturday.
The issue comes after years of delays of Boeing's Max planes following safety and manufacturing crises, including the two deadly crashes of Max 8 aircraft in 2018 and 2019 that killed 346 people. A flawed flight control software system — which has since been updated — was implicated in both crashes.
There are 2,430 Max aircraft currently in service globally, according to Cirium.

articles.title_orig: Tigers' emotional Justin Verlander leaves final career start to hugs
articles.title_zh: Tigers' emotional Justin Verlander leaves final career start to hugs
articles.content_orig:
DETROIT -- Years from now, when folks mention Vintage Verlander, this is what they’ll mean.
For days, the Tigers had joked about sending Justin Verlander out like Billy Chapel. Never mind that the latter is a fictional character, an aging, once-great Tigers pitcher portrayed by Kevin Costner in the 1999 movie “For Love of the Game” who throws a perfect game on the penultimate day of the season to conclude his career.
Justin Verlander's final MLB start • DYK: JV had stats one can only dream of • 'There's no script': Verlander says goodbye before final start • Verlander, Scherzer or Greinke? We debate • Verlander and Scherzer have one last matter to settle • Verlander, daughter share unforgettable first pitch • JV's backstops share favorite memories • Looking back on Verlander's 3 no-hitters • Justin Verlander's career timeline
Never mind that Verlander hadn’t pitched in a Major League game in six months, hadn’t faced an opposing hitter since June, hadn’t fully healed the hamstring that had bothered him all summer, and had just 21 pitches in a simulated game as a ramp-up for his 557th and final Major League start Saturday against the Pirates. This is Verlander, who in his prime, on this same mound at Comerica Park, could win games on pure will.
No, Verlander didn’t get perfection. But with 5 1/3 innings, six strikeouts and two runs allowed, he went out with a performance that looked like it was scripted in Hollywood, complete with the walk off the mound with his family.
“He pitched five [plus] innings. He was throwing 95. Oh my God,” said Eduardo Valencia, whose walk-off two-run homer completed the script and the ninth-inning comeback for a 4-3 win . Valencia was the first Tigers rookie to hit a walk-off home run while trailing since Lou Whitaker on July, 28, 1978.
The scene had been building since the Tigers’ emotional ceremony Friday night celebrating Verlander’s career. Fans flocked downtown early. Many wore Verlander jerseys -- some new, others bought years ago or handed down.
Verlander’s finale was also his first start as a Tiger at Comerica Park since August 2017, before the trade that sent him to Houston. Verlander Day was an event here, and the image of the former Cy Young winner and MVP walking into the ballpark and through the clubhouse with his headphones on and world tuned out was part of the aura.
Saturday was different. Verlander said he wouldn’t have his headphones on for this one, that he would take time to appreciate everything. When he stepped out of the dugout to begin his warmup routine, the sellout crowd roared. He tipped his cap as he walked towards the bullpen, and did it again as he ran the outfield warning track.
“The vibe in the stadium, from the second I walked out there, was just really incredible,” Verlander said. “It brought back some really fond memories of the days when this ballpark was absolutely raucous every single night.”
Bringing back the Verlander from those days was another matter. Nobody, not even Verlander himself, knew how deep he’d be able to pitch, what kind of stuff he would have. More than any other start in his career, Verlander was leaning on guile, his experience of 556 previous starts and 14,636 previous batters faced. He didn’t want just a batter or two; he wanted a real outing.
Turns out, he still had a lot.
Verlander’s former teammate, Pirates manager Don Kelly, stacked Pittsburgh’s lineup with four left-handed hitters at the top to give him a challenge. Verlander retired them all, fanning Oneil Cruz on a slider for his 3,555th career strikeout to lead off the second inning. He gave up a one-out single to rookie Konnor Griffin, who wasn’t even born when Verlander made his MLB debut in 2005.
Griffin was the first batter to face a pitcher who debuted before he was born since Bryce Harper (born on Oct. 16, 1992) faced Miguel Batista (Apr. 11,1992 debut) on June 6, 2012.
Verlander was visibly pumped, though, when catcher Dillon Dingler threw out Griffin trying to steal second base.
“I told [Dingler] before the game that in my sim game, I simulated a runner on first and I couldn’t go fast [in my delivery],” Verlander said. “I told him, ‘Hey, man, I’m going to be a little slower to the plate than usual.’ And he’s like, ‘Don’t worry, man, I got you.’
“So the first time a guy takes off, to throw him out, I’m like, ‘Hell yeah, man. You do got me.’”
Verlander had been searching for his 95 mph fastball since Spring Training. As he reached back for a two-strike fastball to Henry Davis in the third inning, he found it.
“Coming down to it was what his body could do,” Dingler said. “You knew he was going to give it his all. The way he competed, honestly, it was something I’ll never forget. It was awesome.”
Said Verlander: “I was hoping for a little adrenaline. I think the hardest I threw leading up to this was 92 in the sim game.”
Brandon Lowe broke up Verlander’s scoreless outing, jumping Verlander’s fastball on the first pitch of the fourth inning for a home run. Jacob Gonzalez hit a hanging curveball for another solo homer with two outs in the fifth.
In between, Verlander retired five consecutive batters, fanning three of them, including a slider just off the outside corner that drew a called third strike from plate umpire Laz Diaz, also retiring at season’s end. Verlander threw another 95 mph fastball on his 66th pitch.
“Surreal,” Kelly said. “Talk about a competitor, hasn’t pitched since March and going out throwing 90-plus pitches, hitting 95. I think that it was just a microcosm of his career and the competitor that he is.”
Just as Verlander seemed to be reliving his glory days, it was over. Lowe popped out to Dingler leading off the sixth, manager A.J. Hinch emerged the dugout to make the move, then Verlander’s seven-year-old daughter Genevieve – who threw Friday’s ceremonial first pitch to her dad from the mound – ran to the mound to give her dad a hug .
Teammates circled the mound to give their congratulations, then Verlander descended the dugout steps with his wife and kids.
“I've never really set an expectation for myself,” Verlander said. “Every time I've taken the mound, I give it everything I have until the manager decides to take the ball out of my hand. I hope that if there's one thing that people remember of me, that's it. And today was no different.
“I know you have visions of how you want things to go, and some games reach that vision, the super special ones. I think I hold myself to probably an impossible standard, but I think when I lay my head on my pillow tonight, I think I'll feel like I did everything that I wanted to do today.”
