articles.title_orig: Trump calls Iranian plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz not 'acceptable'
articles.title_zh: Trump calls Iranian plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz not 'acceptable'
articles.content_orig:
President Trump waves to the media on the South Lawn of the White House on September 26, 2026 in Washington, D.C. Trump is traveling to Knoxville, Tennessee to attend the University of Tennessee vs. University of Texas College football game. Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images North America hide caption
President Trump said on Saturday that he was rejecting an Iranian plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump said the deal "would not be acceptable," speaking to reporters as he was departing the White House, without giving further explanation.
"I like making a deal too," he said. "But, I'm not — that deal would not be acceptable."
"They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump added.
Iran made the proposal, which also called for resuming negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, at the United Nations General Assembly meetings in New York this week.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters on Friday that Iran conveyed to the U.S. through Qatar a "concrete seven-day plan" to reopen the strait.
Iran initially closed the strait after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. The repeated closures have caused major disruptions to the world's oil supply.
"If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi said on Friday. "The choice now rests with the United States."
The Iranian proposal is similar to a "memorandum of understanding" agreed upon by the U.S. and Iran back in June . It would have temporarily ended fighting and restarted ceasefire talks.
The MoU gave Iran relief from a U.S. naval blockade. The U.S. eased sanctions and freed up frozen Iranian assets. In return, Iran promised not to seek a nuclear weapon and said it would reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
The June agreement collapsed after disputes over the memo's vague wording, including language related to who would control the strait. The U.S. and Iran resumed strikes soon after.
"The actions that the United States should take are not new," Araghchi said. "They are all already in the MoU. They are already under the commitments of the United States. So we don't see any difficulty to implement them."
In a prerecorded interview with CBS set to air Sunday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran will abide by its commitments and said the U.S. needs to show "that it does not intend to overthrow our government or our administration."
"If the United States agrees to proceed in that way, everything will return to the way it was before," Pezeshkian said to CBS. "Because right now, it's the United States that has blocked our way, and naturally, Iran has also blocked the way from its side. These are things that both sides need to open up first; then we can sit down at the negotiating table and discuss other issues at hand."
Pezeshkian said if the U.S. accepts the Iranian proposal on reopening the strait and resuming nuclear negotiations, Iran would allow U.N. nuclear inspectors to enter the country.

articles.title_zh: CNN says it was left off Air Force One for Trump’s Saturday trip to a college football game
articles.content_orig:
The White House is barring CNN from flying on Air Force One on Saturday as part of the news outlet’s duties covering the president on behalf of major television networks.
CNN had been scheduled to fly aboard the president’s plane on his trip to Tennessee for a college football game as part of the White House TV press pool — a small, rotating group of journalists that cover the president in areas where space is limited and share the information they gather with other TV networks.
The move — announced Friday night in a White House note that lays out the president’s schedule — represents the Trump administration’s latest salvo against CNN and the broader White House press corps. No outlet was listed as replacing CNN, meaning there will be no television pool coverage of his trip.
Last week, President Donald Trump announced he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The move also prevented CNN from flying on Air Force One and fulfilling its scheduled pool duties when Trump traveled to the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
A judge later blocked the administration from enforcing the White House ban on the three outlets and ordered it to restore the credentials of the affected reporters. The status of the White House pool, though, was murkier.
With CNN banned, the other TV outlets — Fox, NBC, ABC and CBS — refused to perform their duties until regular access was restored. But regular coverage resumed on Friday, with CNN serving as part of the pool as Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited the National Archives.
It was unclear how the White House’s move might affect CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s litigation. The outside lawyer representing CNN had previously told anchor Jake Tapper he believed the restoration of the outlets’ access included the White House pool. MS NOW and Politico are a part of separate pool rotations from the five major TV networks.
A judge has given the news organizations until Monday to file a request for a preliminary injunction — which would put Trump’s promised ban on hold for a longer period of time.
A CNN spokesperson declined to comment. CNN has reached out to the White House for comment.
In two posts on Truth Social Saturday morning, Trump said CNN and MS NOW should not be allowed in the White House, calling the organizations “perpetrators of FAKE NEWS.”
Later that morning, as he took questions from reporters while departing for Knoxville, an MS NOW reporter asked Trump if he only wants outlets that support him to be part of the White House press pool, to which Trump responded, “I want real news, not fake news.”
“I love an open, free press. What I don’t like is the fake press,” Trump said as he singled out MS NOW and CNN. “What we don’t want is — we don’t want fake news.”
The Washington Post was first to report the White House’s decision.
The TV pool is the primary way that people around the world watch Trump’s speeches and appearances because it supplies video feeds and information to other news organizations.
“That’s the system that allows the networks to share video of the president with the whole country. If they aren’t there, the pool can’t function,” the current president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, Jacqui Heinrich, said on “Fox News Sunday.”
“And America cannot have state TV,” her guest Weijia Jiang of CBS, who was Heinrich’s predecessor as WHCA president, said.
“That’s what makes America America,” she said. “That’s why we need independent coverage, and that’s why this press pool system has been set up for so long and why it works – because you need independent actors to be able to be the observers.”
Along with the TV pool, there are also print, radio and still photography pools. This system exists partly because presidents travel and speak in places where the wider press corps cannot be present.
The Trump White House also produces its own content, including live streams of events.
But, as Jiang put it, “if the government is only showing you what it wants, then you have to question, what are we missing? And that’s what the pool, that’s what these outlets bring to the table.”
This story has been updated with additional details.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier joins 'Varney & Co.' to discuss the state's lawsuit against TikTok, alleging the platform violated Florida's child social media law and endangered minors.
Alabama teenagers using TikTok will soon face two-hour daily limits, overnight curfews and an end to the app's customized "For You" page after the social media giant reached a $100 million settlement with the state.
TikTok reached the first-of-its-kind settlement just days before the lawsuit was scheduled to go to trial. Rather than imposing only financial penalties, the agreement requires the company to overhaul several of its core features for minors.
"TikTok has agreed to give parents real control over what their kids see and how much time they spend on the app," Republican Attorney General Steve Marshall said in a statement. "We've said from day one that our number one goal was to stand up for Alabamians when they are being harmed, and today, we did exactly that."
FLORIDA SUES NETFLIX, ALLEGES STREAMER TRACKED CHILDREN AFTER PROMISING FAMILIES PRIVACY
TikTok said the settlement reflects its ongoing efforts to improve safety features for teens.
"TikTok's priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community," a TikTok USDS Joint Venture spokesperson said. "This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens."
Marshall filed the lawsuit against TikTok in April 2025, alleging the company intentionally designed the app to keep children scrolling while misleading parents about its safety features and the risks it posed to minors.
The lawsuit alleged TikTok's recommendation algorithm exposed children to content involving self-harm, eating disorders, suicide, drugs and sexually explicit material, while overstating the effectiveness of tools such as Restricted Mode and age-verification features.
Within 45 days, TikTok must implement sweeping changes to how minors use the app. Among the most significant is disabling the personalized "For You" page for children. The algorithm-driven feed, which recommends videos based on a user's viewing habits, is widely considered the centerpiece of TikTok's engagement strategy.
The TikTok app logo is shown on an iPhone on Friday, Jan. 17, 2025, in Houston. (AP Photo/Ashley Landis / AP Newsroom)
The agreement also imposes two-hour daily limits, overnight curfews, mandatory "productive pauses" after 15 minutes of continuous use and then another pause at 60 and 90 minutes, bans cosmetic filters for children, strengthens age-verification measures and adds new safeguards limiting interactions between teen and adult accounts.
FEDERAL EMPLOYEES CAN DOWNLOAD TIKTOK ON GOVERNMENT DEVICES AFTER BYTEDANCE'S DIVESTITURE, DOJ SAYS
The changes are intended to curb addictive use among minors and strengthen protections for young users. If TikTok fails to comply with the settlement, the company could face an additional $300 million penalty.
The website for ByteDance Ltd.'s TikTok app is displayed on a smartphone in an arranged photograph in Beijing, China, on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2020. (Photographer: Yan Cong/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
The settlement marks the latest setback for TikTok, which has faced bipartisan scrutiny in Washington for years. Although the social media platform avoided a nationwide U.S. ban earlier this year after its Chinese parent company agreed to divest control of its American operations, it continues to face lawsuits and ongoing questions over children's safety and date privacy.

Trump, Iran’s Pezeshkian set for ‘dramatic’ UNGA as Washington restricts Tehran’s delegation, former White House official warns.
President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are set to converge on New York City for the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) this week, setting up what former White House officials describe as a "dramatic" diplomatic moment, with Tehran’s delegation effectively "captive" under U.S. restrictions amid heightened Middle East tensions.
Pezeshkian, for one, is scheduled to address the assembly on Wednesday, Reuters and Iran's semi-official news agency, Mehr, reported Sunday, with Trump at the rostrum on Tuesday.
"The choreography here is going to make for a fairly dramatic moment," Theo Wold , former acting assistant attorney general and White House domestic policy advisor, told Fox News Digital.
PUTIN, XI AND IRAN'S PEZESHKIAN DESCEND ON INDIA FOR HIGH-STAKES BRICS SUMMIT AMID ESCALATING GLOBAL TENSIONS
President Donald Trump addresses the 80th United Nations General Assembly in New York, Sept. 23, 2025. (Reuters/Shannon Stapleton)
"For the Iranians, the limitation is going to be that there's going to be less access to the international press and less ability for them to essentially poke the Trump administration in the eye," Wold added before noting that it is "pretty sensible to allow them to participate in the international forum and to discuss whatever issues they think are pertinent to their regime and then tell them to go home."
The high-profile gathering also comes as Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran amid the almost seven-month war. Tehran, meanwhile, has set seven conditions for talks with Washington, according to Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei .
Iran also warned on Sunday against any big new attack by the United States and its allies, saying it had information such a move was being prepared, Reuters reported.
While the U.S. approved visas for Iran’s delegation earlier this week, including Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, the State Department has placed strict limits on Iranian movements while in Manhattan.
As the host country under a 1947 U.N. agreement, the United States generally must facilitate the entry and transit of foreign representatives traveling to U.N. headquarters , including officials from adversarial nations.
"While ordinary Iranians endure brutal repression, water and electricity shortages, and soaring inflation, the regime's officials want to go on shopping sprees in New York. Not on our watch," U.S. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said on X.
UN WATCHDOG SLAMS POTENTIAL ELECTION OF IRAN TO PANEL WITH HUMAN RIGHTS SWAY: 'LUNATICS RUNNING THE ASYLUM'
Pezeshkian accused the U.S. of a "grave betrayal" at the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 24, 2025, in New York City. (Jeenah Moon/Reuters)
For Washington, Wold said the U.S. is not obligated to give them unrestricted access beyond diplomatic responsibilities.
"Here, the delegation will be restricted to their accommodation in New York City and the U.N. headquarters there in Manhattan," Wold clarified.
He characterized the move by Washington as a way of telling the delegation it could participate in official discussions but not "go and buy a bunch of microwaves or a small car at Costco or a dealership in the greater New York area."
"Some of the restrictions fully recognize that when Iran comes to New York for UNGA, really it's about them lining their pockets and going on shopping sprees to get household appliances and Rolex watches," Wold said. "They're not going to be going on shopping sprees. They're certainly not going to be hitting up Michelin-starred restaurants in greater Manhattan.
"They also go to Sam’s Club and Walmart and Costco. And that was one of the specific prohibitions issued by the State Department this week: to contact those big-box retailers that require a basic membership and say, ‘You’re not to transact or do any business with Iranians when they arrive, and you’re to notify us when they do.’"
KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian walks to meet with France's President Emmanuel Macron during the General Assembly at U.N. headquarters in New York City on Sept. 24, 2025. (Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images)
Despite the restrictions, Wold said UNGA gives Washington the opportunity it has "wanted for quite some time to have a large enough audience, and a sort of captive Iranian delegation" to make some of the essential points for why the administration pursued the actions it did against the Iranian regime.
Iranian state media also reported Sept. 19 that Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said New York held "absolutely no charm" for the Iranian delegation.
Baghaei, Mehr News Agency reported, went on to accuse the U.S. of using every tool to block the delegation’s participation, asserting that Iran’s attendance is a legal right rather than a favor.
Wold went on to criticize the U.N. for hosting state representatives hostile to American interests while raising security concerns.
"It's going to be one of those things that's fairly perplexing to most Americans," Wold said. "How is it that the representatives of what we have long identified as a hostile regime, but now one that we're actually engaged in combat operations against, one that has killed American service members, why is it that their diplomats get to come to the United Nations and exchange niceties with other kleptocrats or some of their other allies on the international scene?"
TWO US SERVICE MEMBERS KILLED IN IRANIAN STRIKES ON JORDAN, CENTCOM SAYS
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, left, shakes hands with the U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres during the General Assembly on Sept. 25, 2025, in New York City. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
Wold also added that the United Nations wants to "lecture us about international climate change or the need to trans children, but the other is happy to sort of serve as a forum for obvious violators of human rights and obvious regimes that are contrary to any number of internationally agreed-upon protocols."
Amid the hostility between Washington and Tehran, Wold said the gathering could also provide an opening for diplomacy. Trump is also slated to hold bilateral and sideline meetings with leaders from the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) to discuss regional security and the Strait of Hormuz .
"There's the hope that there'll be an opportunity for real discussion," Wold said of UNGA. "Everyone's hope, especially from State Department leadership, is that there'll be an opportunity to have a fulsome, sort of meaningful discussion with the Iranians, freed from some of the theatrics the Iranians have engaged in.

"There's a hope that there'll be an opportunity for closed-door private discussions between the United States and Iranians and really try to hammer out some kind of agreement about what a cessation of hostilities will look like."
Wold expressed confidence in Washington’s posture heading into the summit.
"The president is best equipped for these moments. This is really where he sort of shines as a natural leader," he said. "He's not one to bend or to break. It's a precarious time for President Trump, but I have no doubt at all that he'll rise to the moment."

The ending was extremely ugly, but the Horns escaped Knoxville undefeated.
The first on-campus meeting between two college football blue bloods is happening in Knoxville as the No. 1 Texas Longhorns take on the No. 14 Tennessee Volunteers at Neyland Stadium on Saturday.
It’s a big test for Texas senior quarterback Arch Manning, who was not able to win a true road game in regulation in 2025, his first season as the starter, and for a Longhorns team trying to maintain its hold on the top ranking as it embarks on a nine-game SEC schedule full of ranked opponents.
Texas senior running back Hollywood Smothers went through warmups for the Horns after his removal from the injury report, but came up gimpy at the end in the wake of suffering a lower-body injury. Also available is junior edge Colin Simmons, who suffered a toe injury last week before going through warmups with a large brace on his elbow.
After winning the toss and deferring to the second half, Tennessee kicked off to Texas, which started with an eight-yard completion to junior wide receiver Ryan Wingo on a comeback before runs by fifth-year Raleek Brown and freshman Derrek Cooper secured the first down after the spot on Cooper’s effort was overturned in favor of the Longhorns.
Looking for a shot play to junior wide receiver Emmet Mosley, Manning didn’t deliver a pretty pass, but it was effective for a 43-yard gain.
A tackle for loss on Brown initially put Texas behind the chains before a penalty for 12 men on the field gave the Longhorns a 1st and 5 inside the red zone. Manning took a big hit delivering a check down to freshman wide receiver Jermaine Bishop that was good for another first down. Trying to secure tough yardage, a tough run by Brown picked up three yards before Brown scored on a nine-yard touchdown run behind a good insert block by Wingo.
A missed tackle by senior safety Jelani McDonald allowed a short pass by Tennessee quarterback Faizon Brandon to turn into a first down with 15 yards added on for a roughing the passer penalty on sophomore defensive end Lance Jackson. The Volunteers took a shot play on the next snap and senior cornerback Bo Mascoe was called for pass interference on an underthrown ball by Brandon.
Tennessee picked up two yards on a run by DeSean Bishop, a quarterback run by Brandon, and a toss to Bishop picked up a big first down into the Texas red zone before the run defense of the Longhorns limited Bishop to a one-yard gain and a short scramble by Brandon set up 3rd and 7. With time in the pocket, Brandon missed an open receiver, but was able to avoid a sack, throwing the ball away to preserve a 33-yard field goal that split the uprights.
In 10 personnel to start the next drive, Texas senior right tackle Melvin Siani was beat for a sack to put the Longhorns well behind the chains, leading to a six-yard completion to Cooper and an illegal forward pass on Manning when he got caught between scrambling and tossing the ball out to Brown, whose first down was negated by penalty.
The fourth penalty on Texas, an illegal formation on the punt, moved the ball from the Tennessee 37-yard line to the 42-yard line to start the second drive for the Volunteers.
Once again, Brandon was able to avoid a sack, but took a loss flipping the ball out to the perimeter, where senior linebacker Rasheem Biles made the tackle for a loss. On 3rd and 12, Texas finally got Brandon to the ground after the freshman quarterback didn’t rip a throw and Simmons came up with the sack to force a punt that senior Ryan Niblett returned for 10 yards to the 33-yard line.
Back to a heavier package, the 12 personnel look only produced a two-yard gain by Brown, setting up a play-action pass that Manning completed to Wingo, who sat down in an open spot in the zone coverage for a 15-yard gain. A better run by Brown netted five yards before Wingo broke multiple tackles on a screen pass to pick up 14 yards on one of the best post-catch efforts by Wingo in his Longhorns career.
When sophomore left guard Dylan Sikorski was beat on a slant, Cooper was dropped for a three-yard loss to put Texas off schedule, but Manning responded with a beautiful throw to Bishop on a corner route that was misplayed by the Tennessee secondary for a 29-yard gain to the 5-yard line.
Under pressure, Manning couldn’t hit junior wide receiver Cam Coleman on a jump ball and more pressure resulted in a sack of the Texas quarterback to end the first quarter.
Trying to work the perimeter with Brown wasn’t effective against the speed of the Tennessee defense, and Texas had to settle for a 22-yard field goal by senior Gianni Spetic for a 10-3 lead.
A two-yard completion prior to a designed run for no gain left Brandon down on the grass banged up and favoring his left shoulder when he was finally escorted off the field and into the injury tent.
With the backup quarterback in an 3rd and 8, Tennessee couldn’t create separation and Georgia MacIntyre had to scramble for a short gain as the Volunteers had to punt. On another good punt return by Niblett that went for 20 yards, it was Tennessee flagged for an illegal formation to allow Texas to start its drive on its 43-yard line.
On second down, Manning tried to hit a shot play to Coleman, but threw into double coverage and the ball was intercepted at the Tennessee 4-yard line.
Trying to create space off the goal line, Bishop ran for three yards on first down and MacIntyre completed a pass for a fresh set of downs. Patience working off the left side of the Tennessee line, Bishop picked up four yards and MacIntyre threw it away after standing in a clean pocket for a lengthy period of time. On 3rd and 6, MacIntyre came under quick pressure from fifth-year defensive tackle Hero Kanu and had to throw it away again.
Niblett continued to look dangerous on a 14-yard return negated by a block in the back penalty on junior Jordon Johnson-rubell that moved the ball back to the Texas 39-yard line.
A bad snap by fifth-year center Connor Robertson resulted in a 12-yard loss instead of a turnover when Manning was able to rip the ball away at the bottom of the pile. When Brown picked up four yards on a run and the Texas quarterback took a big hit on an 11-yard scramble for a three and out. Tennessee took over at its 8-yard line after a 51-yard punt by Mac Chiumento.
Brandon returned to the field after spending 15 minutes in the injury tent and ran for seven yards on first down, then completed a two-yard pass. On 3rd and 1, Tennessee ran for a first down behind two tight ends side by side in the backfield. When senior Brad Spence lost contain on the edge, Brandon was able to scramble for a first down before getting sacked by junior defensive tackle Maraad Watson. A one-yard gain set up 3rd and 13 after a timeout by Texas because too many players were on the field as head coach Steve Sarkisian avoided a penalty.
Simmons sacked Brandon on third down and the Volunteers were ready to punt, but Simmons was called for unsportsmanlike conduct for a vulgar celebration after the play that gave Tennessee a first down and enough momentum to pick up chunk gains of 10 yards, eight yards, 10 yards, and 13 yards before the Texas defense recovered enough to get a run stuff and force an incompletion by Brandon, who didn’t gain much on a quarterback draw on third down prior to the two-minute timeout.
Just outside of field-goal range, Tennessee head coach Josh Heupel went for it on 4th and 7 and Brandon took a shot, but physical play and good positioning from sophomore nickel back Graceson Littleton resulted in a turnover on downs.
The Longhorns opened the drive by giving up a big loss against a run blitz and Manning was flagged again for an illegal forward pass. Decisive enough to actually scramble instead of getting caught in between, Manning picked up 13 yards, but was seven yards short of the first down for a second straight three and out.
Tennessee took over at its own 22-yard line with 51 seconds and two timeouts remaining. B

articles.content_orig:
Boeing said it flagged a software glitch last month on some 737 Max aircraft that could affect certain landing procedures, as the manufacturer seeks federal approval for the fourth and final model in its best-selling aircraft family.
The Federal Aviation Administration said Saturday that it is assessing the problem and "will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern" and that it will review Boeing's proposed fix.
Boeing said the issue could arise after a missed approach when pilots alter a preprogrammed flight path, and that pilots must take additional steps to use automated tools on subsequent approaches.
"We shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases. Our engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue," Boeing said. The Wall Street Journal reported the issue earlier.
The company said that pilots are trained to land without the automated system. "We are working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur," Boeing said.
U.S. airlines told CNBC that they do not have Max 8 and Max 9 airplanes with the updated software tied to the glitch in their fleets. Airlines can revert some Maxes to the older software version.
All-Boeing 737 Max carrier Southwest Airlines said it is "aware of the issue and is engaged with Boeing and the FAA."
It added that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes." United Airlines also said it's not taking any Max aircraft deliveries with the new software.
However, questions remain about the two other models, the Max 7 and Max 10. The Federal Aviation Administration certified the Max 7 , the smallest of the Max family, in early August with the newest software installed. It wasn't immediately clear if the aircraft could be delivered or fly with an older version of software.
Additionally, Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors earlier this month that he expected FAA certification of the Max 10 "very soon."
"We have been engaged with Boeing and the FAA and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps," Alaska Airlines , a Max 10 customer, said Saturday.
The issue comes after years of delays of Boeing's Max planes following safety and manufacturing crises, including the two deadly crashes of Max 8 aircraft in 2018 and 2019 that killed 346 people. A flawed flight control software system — which has since been updated — was implicated in both crashes.
There are 2,430 Max aircraft currently in service globally, according to Cirium.
